speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NUCLEAR TESTING
subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO U.K. GOVERNMENT
speechtext: wish to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the announcement by the United Kingdom government that they intend to conduct an underground nuclear test, and in view of the Canadian government's declared opposition to nuclear testing by any power, will the minister tell the house whether any representations have been made by his department to the government of the United Kingdom regarding this decision, or has the hon. gentleman any comments to make in this regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NUCLEAR TESTING
subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO U.K. GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
There have been no representations made to the British government, but Canada's position on the question of nuclear testing is clearly understood by all of the governments concerned. The United Kingdom conducted a similar test last March 1 as part of a joint program with the United States. They have now announced their intention to explode another device, but the British minister of defence, Mr. Thorneycroft, has stated that this is in no sense the start of a new series.
At this time all the nuclear powers are engaged in testing programs, either in the atmosphere or underground. As I have said, Canada's opposition to the continuation of these tests has been clearly stated in this house and at the United Nations. It is for this reason our delegation played a leading part in working for the adoption of a United Nations resolution which would assist in providing a basis for an end to testing.
None of the major powers, the nuclear powers, voted against that resolution. They agreed to the early reconvening of the 18 nation disarmament committee for the purpose of resuming negotiations on the cessation of nuclear testing in particular, and the committee is asked to report back to the general assembly by December 10. I believe the 18 nation committee will be meeting in Geneva within the next ten days, and I do not by any means rule out the possibility that during this next intensive round of negotiations in Geneva an agreement will be reached which will put a stop to all testing.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the government proposes to maintain its decision to withdraw from the international committee for European migration?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN SUPPORT OF COMMITTEE FOR EUROPEAN MIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an answer ready for that question. In view of recent press reports concerning Canada's withdrawal from the intergovernmental committee for European migration, it seems advisable to set out the reasons which led to Canada's decision to resign. ICEM, of course, is not a United Nations body but is a committee of some 30 governments. I might add that Canada is not the only country to withdraw from the organization. Sweden resigned last year. Canada's decision to withdraw was taken only after a most

careful review of all relevant factors, and was concurred in by the various departments concerned.
Canada was one of the founding members of ICEM, which was formed in 1951 to meet the problems created by refugees and nonrefugee surplus populations in Europe after world war II. At that time there were large numbers of European refugees living in camps awaiting resettlement opportunities. The problem of non-refugee surplus populations was still critical for a number of European countries, where it tended to be one of the factors impeding economic development. ICEM facilitated the transport of refugee and non-refugee migrants from European countries with surplus populations to countries overseas welcoming increased immigration. In the years from 1951 to 1961 ICEM played a very useful role in the resettlement overseas of refugees and migrants.

subtopic: CANADIAN SUPPORT OF COMMITTEE FOR EUROPEAN MIGRATION
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the minister, who is giving very valuable information, but this is more of a long, reasoned answer than the kind of answer expected on orders of the day. subtopic: CANADIAN SUPPORT OF COMMITTEE FOR EUROPEAN MIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will leave what I have already said to be reported under motions and I will go on with the rest of my statement.
However, toward the end of world refugee year in 1961 when, under United Nations auspices, an intensified effort was made to deal with refugee problems, it became apparent that the refugee problem had been substantially reduced. There are now just a few thousand refugees living in camps, and it is expected that these will be resettled in the very near future. In North America and Europe and elsewhere there are signs that we are returning to a more normal activity in the field of migration. The European economy now seems capable of absorbing most of the surplus population in that continent without international assistance.
Inquiries of the Ministry
As far as Canada is concerned we prefer- and I think this has been the policy down through the years-to rely on bilateral arrangements and on our own immigration facilities. In normal times Canada is not persuaded that national migration requires or justifies by itself the existence of an international agency. This is the essence of the reason why Canada is withdrawing.
Very little use of ICEM's services has been made by Canada over the years. None the less, Canadian participation in ICEM has involved an annual assessment of approximately $200,000. In addition, in the past few years a grant of $60,000 has been made to the refugee transport program of ICEM. While financial considerations were not the primary reason for Canada's withdrawal, it has become increasingly difficult to justify paying such a price for an organization of marginal use to Canada.
For the reasons I have given and because other international commitments have assumed a greater priority, the government decided that Canadian participation in ICEM should be terminated. This decision in no way diminishes Canadian interest in refugee problems, an interest which will continue to be reflected in Canada's support in the United Nations for programs of assistance to refugees. Canada is one of the main contributors to the work carried on by the United Nations high commissioner for refugees. In addition, the government intends to examine from year to year the question of continuing a special voluntary grant of $60,000 to the refugee transport fund of ICEM.

I am informed that the defence research board, in consultation with expert seismologists of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, has examined the proposals made at the so-called 1962 Pugwash conference. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, November 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-3, to amend the Food and Drugs Act-Mr. Monteith-Mr. Chown in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
When the committee rose last evening we were considering clause 3 [Mr. Orlikow.l
of the bill and the amendment proposed thereto by the hon. member for Halton. Is the committee ready for the question on the proposed amendment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
No.
On clause 3-

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked if I would outline the authority which the present act and the proposed legislation gives in connection with the withdrawal of a drug from the market.
The clause which is contained in the bill prohibiting the sale of a drug listed in schedule H automatically would confer authority to seize such a drug where an inspector, on reasonable grounds, believed that a provision of the act had been violated. This requires us to look at the definition of "sell" which includes "offer for sale, expose for sale, have in possession for sale and distribute". If a drug were added to schedule H it would be in violation of the act for a pharmacist to offer it for sale, expose it for sale or even to have it in possession for sale, and an inspector would therefore be within his authority in seizing that drug under those circumstances. Similarly in the case of a drug in the hands of a member of one of the professions. Here the element of sale does not arise so directly, but the word "distribute" could well be invoked to authorize an inspector to seize a schedule H drug if a physician was distributing that drug. I have already mentioned the authority to exempt such a drug for limited purposes, and this could be invoked where necessary for research and so on.
It is felt that the present act and the proposed amendment give ample authority to deal with any practical problems that might arise in connection with the necessity to remove a schedule H drug from the market. A different question, however, was posed in connection with the right to remove a drug from the possession of a doctor, dentist, veterinary surgeon or pharmacist. This, for the reasons pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River, would go far beyond anything which is presently contained in the Food and Drugs Act and could be challenged on the ground that it went beyond the requirements of the criminal law and invaded a field that was provincial.
While I do not think any great difficulty would lie in securing the ready withdrawal of a drug from the market, and indeed our experience has shown that there would be no problem under the legislation as it is being amended, this may be a convenient time at which to place beyond any question

the right to remove a drug under certain limited conditions. I think it would be an unwarranted interference with medical practice and the right of a physician to determine his use of a drug to provide authority, even if this were possible, to take it away from him. By the same token, if complete protection were to be afforded it would also be necessary to seize or remove a drug from the possession of a private citizen. This, I suggest, would pose problems which go far beyond any practical necessity.
Because in the case of new drugs a physician's initial supplies may likely be obtained through the sampling regulations, I would be prepared to consider some authority which would give the right to the governor in council to make regulations respecting the withdrawal of these drugs if they are found sufficiently dangerous to warrant their being placed in schedule H. In other words, I would be prepared to see an amendment to the bill which would permit the governor in council to make regulations respecting the withdrawal of a drug listed in schedule H that had been furnished by way of sample. This is an area which, I think, clearly could be justified under our authority concerning the distribution of drug samples. It would not interfere with ownership, because they are in each case furnished free and subject to conditions, one of which could be an agreement that it be returned in the event that it was found necessary subsequently to put it into schedule H.
I think with the explanation I have given, and the authority which I have suggested might be contained in the act, we would be in a position to deal with any eventuality that might arise where the danger of a drug had been sufficiently established to require its addition to schedule H. Once the drug had been placed in schedule H, then its sale would automatically be prohibited and the withdrawal machinery whereby the recipient of the sample had agreed to return it would become operative. I think this would fully cover all possible situations and, in my view is as far as we could go in dealing with such an eventuality.
I trust this proposal will be satisfactory to the hon. member who had put forward an amendment to clause 3 and had asked that I explore some alternative wording to cover the situation he had in mind. I think this does that, and an amendment to provide authority in the regulations is being presented by my colleague the Minister of Public Works. In the meantime, I wonder whether the hon. member for Halton would agree to
Food and Drugs Act
withdraw his amendment, and then I would be happy to ask my colleagues to propose the one I have suggested.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
I wholeheartedly agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. This particular clause of the bill before us covers such a wide area of the problem in relation to these drugs that we should go further into the matter and scrutinize every aspect of it. After all, Mr. Chairman, we in this committee want to give to the people of Canada the best possible Food and Drugs Act, and I do not think that with the information available to this committee we have sufficient material to study the question properly. The United States congress on October 4 of this year amended the food and drug act of that country after two years of exhaustive study of the drug industry, and I believe that in two days we just are not capable of doing anything which would equalize their magnificent effort.
Mr. Chairman, I draw your attention to the words "testing of any new drug" which are to be found in clause 3. I believe this is the crux of the whole drug problem, especially in view of the thalidomide tragedy in Canada. It has been brought to the attention of the governments involved in the thalidomide tragedy that so far these drugs have not gone through a comprehensive test, especially in the preclinical stage, and above all in the important matter of testing drugs for teratogenicity. Dr. Helen Taussig of John Hopkins University has reviewed several X-ray films of rats fed with the drug thalidomide, and she found that the foetuses of these pregnant rats did contain malformations of limbs, so called phocomelia.
At this stage of the discussion of the bill I think the minister owes to this committee answers to several questions with regard to the testing of new drugs. The first question is whether the food and drug directorate conduct any tests at all in their laboratories as far as teratogenicity is concerned. Second, do the food and drug directorate demand any information on teratogenicity of new drugs from the manufacturing drug houses themselves? Third, have the food and drug directorate a resolution demanding that all drug manufacturers be licensed in this country? I believe that if there are drug manufacturers in this country who are not licensed, this can only work to the detriment of the people of Canada. After all, doctors

have to be licensed, pharmacists have to be licensed, engineers have to be licensed, and I think it is very important that drug manufacturers should have to be licensed before they manufacture and distribute drugs in this country. Furthermore, I believe that even distributors of drugs should be licensed, as well as importers of drugs from other countries. Otherwise how are we to get an assurance that the drugs available in Canada come from ethical companies, ethical distributors and ethical importers?
Mr. Chairman, I think I will now give the minister a chance to reply to these questions, and then I will carry on from there.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am informed that there were no tests for teratogenicity prior to December 1, 1961, but that now we do demand, and have demanded, information concerning teratogenicity from manufacturers. That has been so prior to December 1 and since.
Mr. Chairman, all these matters will be given further consideration. As I mentioned last evening, we are expecting the report of the committee of the royal college of physicians and surgeons quite soon, and as soon as it it received naturally we will act on it. I am not saying that everything recommended in the report will be accepted 100 per cent, but there will certainly be some recommendations on which we will be acting, and at that time we will take into consideration all of the angles with regard to new drugs and new drug procedures, and as to when and how we accept a drug for distribution and permit it to be used in Canada. Incidentally, this bill is drawn up to provide the necessary authority to implement the report of the special committee of the royal college of physicians and surgeons when it is received.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, is this committee to believe that when this report is brought in we will be notified of all the recommendations they bring forward for consideration of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext: I am told I would have to ask for the consent of the royal college of physicians and surgeons to table this report, but this would be my intention; and certainly any regulations implemented as a result of the report would be done automatically by order in council and would appear in the Canada Gazette. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
Then I gather, Mr. Chairman, judging from the reply of the minister, that all that we, the elected representatives of the people, will be allowed to do is to read

the regulations in the Canada Gazette, and we will not have an opportunity to discuss in the house any new regulations under the Food and Drugs Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext: This is standard procedure in instances of this kind. Of course if somebody has a question to raise they can put a motion on the order paper and can discuss it. I would think there would be ample opportunity, when the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare come up for consideration, to discuss any matter having to do with the department, including regulations.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think this is totally inadequate. 1 think the amendments to this Food and Drugs Act are of very great importance to the people of Canada, and I think we, the elected representatives of the people, being concerned with public safety in Canada, should scrutinize the recommendations which the royal college will be presenting to the government before they become law. Otherwise we shall have again this government by order in council tradition.
In view of these facts I think it is extremely important that we should refer this whole matter to a special committee of the house, where we could have expert advice, and where we the members of this House of Commons would be able to question experts in the drug industry. Otherwise, as I see it, all the work is being done by a few men appointed by the royal college of physicians and surgeons.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext: This is completely wrong, Mr. Chairman. It is ridiculous to say that all this work is going to be done by the royal college of physicians and surgeons. This special committee of the royal college is presenting a report to me as minister. From that report we come up with the regulations which we feel to be consistent with their effort and for the good and the welfare of the people of Canada. After these regulations have been enacted they appear in the Canada Gazette. They have done so by order in council. At any time on my estimates I am quite free to discuss these regulations after they have been enacted.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext: I think the minister has led us into some confusion. He has said the regulations would be drafted so as to be consistent with that report. Perhaps he meant that the regulations would be consistent with the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

speechtext:
That is better.
Food and Drugs Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext: The minister will think I have a one track mind, but sometimes this is not a bad attribute. In reading over yesterday's transcript of the work of the committee I am still not clear on one point, and I wonder whether the minister could clear it up. It is still bothering some of us. The question is whether there is embodied in these amendments or implicit in them any authority for the health and drug directorate to remove supplies of drugs at the drug store level, with respect to any drugs that are put under schedule H. speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

Another purpose is concerning schedule H, the prohibition of sale. Clause 3 is the one we are dealing with now, and simply provides for regulations or gives us authority so that we may make regulations concerning new drugs primarily, which we expect to be reviewed in the report. As I said earlier, it is up to the department to develop the regulations, but this will be done in consideration of the report of the royal college of physicians and surgeons. Then, of course, clause 4 contains reference to two drugs, namely thalidomide and lysergic acid. Actually there is nothing in this act concerning licensing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

If I understood him correctly he said the act gave him authority to withdraw drugs from a drug store, for instance, providing that drug store was actually offering them for sale, but that in the event of those drugs being within that drug store and not being offered for sale, he then had not authority to withdraw them. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS

I am told that this would be a matter of interpretation. I presume if they were down in the basement of a drug store and were stored away, they would not be offered

Food and Drugs Act
for sale. However, if they were in any position where it could be interpreted that they were being offered for sale, we would then have every power to pick them up.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTROL AND REGULATION OF CERTAIN DRUGS
speechtext:
There seem to be several points of confusion in this debate. I think one of them is that we are trying to be helpful and the minister does not quite appreciate that fact.
First may I say that it is to me a source of confusion that when members of the opposition propose amendments in order to enable the department to gather in supplies of harmful drugs, it is argued from the government benches that this provision might be invading the field of property and civil rights and therefore be ultra vires of the powers of this parliament. On the other hand when we press the minister, in certain instances he reminds us of the other clause in the act that gives the government power under certain circumstances to seize some of these supplies. I suggest that is a sample of the kind of confusion we have in this debate.
The thing which it seems to me ought to impress itself on the mind of the minister is the experience he had during the thalidomide crisis. His department desired not only to stop the sale and distribution of thalidomide, but to get all the supplies back from wherever they were. He argued that there was some doubt as to whether the government had authority to do this. It is even suggested to this date that the action taken may not have had proper legal authority. What we are trying to do is suggest to the minister that there be put into the act legal authority to enable the government to do in another such crisis what it did, whether or not it had authority to do so, in the thalidomide crisis.
So far as the thalidomide crisis is concerned, I think the government is to be commended for taking the action it took. The letters that were written and the directives that were sent out must have been drafted by some fairly smart lawyers. They did not offend the law, yet they produced the result. As I say, we are trying to be helpful. We are trying to suggest to the minister that he accept the offer of members of this house to have put into the act the necessary authority so that any drug-whether it is a sample, a new drug or an old drug-that is found to be harmful, be a drug that the government can withdraw from any place in which it may be.
We do not know what the next crisis in this field will be. As I think the minister pointed out in his speech on second reading when this debate started some weeks ago, it sometimes happens in the field of science,

and in the field of medical science in particular, that as we move ahead and discover things that are a boon to human life, things can happen that cause a crisis along the way. As medical science develops new drugs that may be exceedingly helpful, drugs that may cure some of the diseases that are still regarded as incurable, there may be another crisis such as the one we had in respect of thalidomide. I wish the minister would realize that those in the various opposition groups who are pressing him to take some action in this field are of one mind with him, of one mind with the department in the attitude they took to the thalidomide crisis. I wish, therefore, he would be a little more appreciative of the things we are trying to present than he has been thus far.
The hon. member for Halton is not wedded to the wording he put forward last night. He has withdrawn those words. None of us is wedded to any form of words. As a matter of fact the hon. member for York South, the nearest legal adviser I have, has drafted some words for me that I could put forward. I do not intend to do so at this moment because I do not believe this is the place to try to settle the exact form of the wording. I think this is the place for us to deal with the principle of whether or not the government should have this kind of authority. The house, in my view, should give the government the authority to do what it did in the thalidomide crisis when that authority was not there.
If I might use the same words I used the last time I was on my feet, I would say this underlines very strongly the need for this bill to be referred to a standing or special committee. The minister would shorten this debate greatly if he would solve the riddle for us as to whether that is going to happen. He told us when he opened the debate on second reading back in October, and when he closed the debate yesterday, it was his view that we should deal with this matter first of all in committee of the whole. Then, as I recall his words, if it was the sense of the house or if it seemed desirable that it should go to a standing committee, that could be done. If he were to tell us now it is the sense of the house that it should go to a special committee, there would be less time taken on these individual clauses.
While I am on my feet I should like to say a word on another aspect of this subject which is also in support of my contention that the bill should go before a standing or select committee. I refer to the fact that the regulations, under the section with which we are now dealing, are not going to be drafted until after the government receives the report from the special committee of the

royal college of physicians and surgeons. I am not making any complaint about the fact that the government wants to wait until it gets that report before it decides what its new regulations should be regarding the manufacture, packing, storing and testing of new drugs. I think that is wise. I recognize the fact that it is standard procedure for the government to ask parliament to give to the government the power to make regulations which we do not see until later. Usually this is done because we know nothing of what is in the government's mind at this point. In this particular case, the government itself does not know what is in its mind. It is waiting, commendably, until the report comes from the special committee of the royal college of physicians and surgeons.
It seems to me it follows logically, therefore, that all of us should wait until that committee has made its report, until we have these various recommendations, until we have some idea what kind of regulations the government is going to bring down under this section. This is-I do not use this phrase with any heat-blank cheque legislation. I hesitate, being no longer minister of justice, to try what must be interpreted now as an impromptu amateurish effort to assist the committee, but I shall endeavour to do so if the committee will put it on no higher basis than that this is an opinion of an individual member and is not an authoritative statement of the government's view. I think that what the hon. member who has just taken his seat has posed is but the problem which confronts any police officer or law enforcement officer under this act or any other act under the Criminal Code.
The officer concerned, in this case the inspector, has the right to enter premises to see whether or not a breach of a statute is being committed. The statute provides that it is an offence to have certain prescribed articles in possession for the purposes of sale or distribution, or to offer them for sale. The inspector then has to decide whether the circumstances which he finds there constitute a breach of the statute. If he is of the opinion that they do, then he seizes the article in question.
The person in whose premises they are found then of course has the right, when the case comes before the courts-or he can go to the courts himself-to say there was no breach of the statute. The inspector will then

have to adduce evidence to establish that there was a breach, and the courts will decide. It will not be an arbitrary decision of the inspector. It will be subject to review by the courts, and if the courts decide there was a breach of the statute then the seizure is maintained, the articles are forfeited, and whatever penalty is decided will follow.
If the courts decide there was no breach, in other words that the goods were in possession not for the purposes of sale or distribution but in the possession of a private individual for his legitimate purposes, then there is no breach, no forfeiture, and the goods will be restored. But until the courts have decided, the goods will remain seized and will be in the custody of the courts.
That is the situation under any statute under which it becomes the responsibility of a law enforcement officer to see that the law is carried out. It is not his final decision; it is the decision of the courts which determines that question, but the inspector has authority to seize if he believes a breach of the statute is in process.

But, sir, we surely should not, in attempting to remedy or meet a serious situation, go so far as in fact to create a greater evil or impose greater handicaps than we are trying to remedy. If we declared the mere possession of these substances to be an offence we would, for instance, render impossible any experimentation, even the most legitimate and scientific experimentation, for the purpose of research. Therefore I think perhaps we are getting a little bit off the beaten path here in this insistence by the opposition taking the position that these safeguards be instituted, because I think these men are all honourable enough that once they were asked to destroy these drugs, they would realize the drugs should be destroyed. I do not think it is practical for inspectors to go into every office to see that these drugs are removed. I think once they have been declared unlawful, those in possession of them will see that they are not used, and they will be destroyed. In rising to speak on this matter, I speak from the heart and not from notes. I listened last evening and today to the discussion, and I claim I have proper grounds for taking part in this debate because of the fact that for the past 13 years I have been associated with a hospital in Toronto. One of the patients in that hospital is a basket baby, born recently without arms or legs, as a result, it is believed, of the use of this drug thalidomide. The child is still living and is a glorious child.
On Saturday afternoon I spent two hours in company with the doctors of the hospital and, of course, this present debate in parliament, and the condition of the child, were the foremost topics. I was interested to hear those doctors tell me: Don't throw the babies out with the bath water. This drug is a magnificent sedative. If its sale is prohibited in Canada you are taking it away from men and from young people, particularly of the male sex. It is a wonderful sedative. They went so far as to tell me that had Marilyn Monroe taken this drug as a sedative instead of the drug she did, she would be living to this day, because there are no serious after effects following its use as a sedative as there are from some other sleeping pills.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare said yesterday he was not going to rush
Food and Drugs Act
the legislation on this matter, and I believe him. I know the minister, and he is doing a magnificent job in my opinion. I believe him when he says he does not intend to rush this legislation through. I say to him that rat poison is bad for human beings to take, yet we have it on the shelves of the stores. This drug thalidomide is a magnificent sedative and I do not think it should be banned from the shelves of Canada, despite the fact that I have seen the effects of its use by pregnant women. Thalidomide has been a tragedy in Canada and throughout the world because of the birth of deformed babies. Nevertheless, the minister yesterday gave an inkling of the thinking in the medical world on this score. How many people realize that this drug may be the answer to cancer? Research work is being done in this regard today. The growth of the foetus in a pregnant woman is a cellular growth, and it has been proven, through these unfortunate cases, that the use of this particular drug counteracts the natural cellular growth of the foetus. Cancer is also a cellular growth and researchers are now working on the theory that thalidomide may be the answer to cancer. If it is an agent which counteracts the cellular growth of the foetus, might it not be a counteracting agent to the growth of cancer cells?
In the meantime, this drug is of great benefit as a sedative for older men and adolescent men, and I suggest it should be available to the public of Canada under the same conditions as other poisons. The sale of poisons is surrounded by precautions and there could be precautions surrounding the sale of thalidomide to see that pregnant women did not use it. For these reasons I do not think its sale should be banned altogether and its use circumscribed as suggested in the proposals we have heard.
I support in every way the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the whole question be referred to a special committee of the house. I have never been more serious in my life than when discussing this subject. I have seen a baby without arms and legs, and yet I am standing up for the drug. So I think what I have said represents a considered opinion. As I have told the committee, I have seen the effects of this drug; maybe some other hon. members have not. Research teams will continue their work and it may yet be that this drug represents the lightening of the dark cloud which now overhangs the dark world of cancer.

the second reading of Bill No. C-4, to amend the Department of National Health and Welfare Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-4 embodies two amendments to the Department of National Health and Welfare Act. The first is of a routine procedural nature while the second envisages a major step forward in the development of welfare in Canada.
As hon. members are aware, the federal government has long had at its disposal a top level advisory council in the field of health. Consisting of deputy ministers of health, as well as non-governmental representatives, this council has a distinguished record of service to the nation stretching over a period of some 43 years. The council has not only furnished continuing advice and guidance to federal health ministers but has also served as the spearhead of federal-provincial co-operation without which our present pattern of nation-wide health services would have been virtually impossible of achievement. Indeed, an examination of the health council's history indicates the key role which this body has played in many of our greatest successes, such as the development and expansion of the national health grants, the introduction of the Salk polio vaccine, and the implementation of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. In my own case, since becoming minister I have found the health council of great assistance. It has been of substantial help in developing our general health policy and in dealing with the many difficult technical problems which arise from time to time in this field. Certainly, the government and people of Canada owe an important debt of gratitude to this very distinguished Canadian institution.
In view of this council's contribution to Canada's health progress, the government has felt that it would be equally helpful to have a similar body established in the field of welfare. This is the major purpose of the legislation presently before the house. The national council of welfare now being proposed will be in the nature of an advisory body to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, with duties and functions paralleling those of the health council. With its membership being drawn up on a comparable basis, the new council will, we believe, afford social welfare the status which is its due and exert significant influence on future developments

in this field. The timing of the council's establishment is particularly appropriate in view of a further innovation currently being implemented in the welfare field. I am referring to the new program of national welfare grants. As I announced to the house on April 12 last, these grants will cover three important areas-general welfare, professional training and research. They represent a significant departure in the welfare field and it is our hope that the national council of welfare will provide the same kind of support to their development as has the health council in relation to the national health grants.
On previous occasions, I have mentioned the importance of this new council with respect to the improvement of Canada's various social security programs. For many years, we have been sharing with the provinces the cost of old age assistance, disabled and blind persons allowances, and unemployment assistance. We have now clearly reached the point when we must re-examine the mass of complex regulations and procedures that have been developed at different points in our history to meet particular needs. The time has now come for us to take a fresh look at this whole field with a view to developing a more consistent and integrated approach to public assistance in Canada.
I might mention one or two examples of the kind of problem which will be referred to the new council. There is the question of additional aid for the blind, which has been raised by organizations representing the blind in Canada. There is the question of the most appropriate approach with respect to the provision of aid under our federal-provincial assistance programs. The categorical programs covering old age assistance, blind and disabled persons allowances have an income and property test and a maximum benefit. Unemployment assistance, on the other hand, operates on the basis of a budgetary approach to need and has no upper limit under the federal legislation. Different views have been expressed as to the most appropriate method of providing federal aid under these measures, and we are anxious to obtain the best and most representative advice with respect to this matter.
I might say that the provinces have also expressed the view that these joint programs should be reassessed. At the dominion-provincial conference in the fall of 1960, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated the need for further study in order that these measures might be simplified and, if possible, consolidated to some extent. The new national council of welfare will, I believe, provide a vehicle through which these matters may be considered. The nature and scope of
Health and Welfare Act the federal legislation affects the administrative operations of the provincial authorities. It would be most helpful in this regard to have on this advisory council the administrators of provincial programs, who will be in a position to make suggestions leading to greater administrative simplicity and efficiency. In addition, the background of these administrators in meeting day-to-day welfare problems in all walks of life should prove particularly valuable to the council. Their presence on the council should facilitate further federal-provincial liaison in the administration of programs and expedite the exchange of information and the discussion of common problems on a regular basis. Another matter of great importance which the council will be asked to consider has to do with the introduction of an old age, survivors and disability insurance program together with the relationship such a program will have to existing provincial and federal-provincial programs.
As hon. members are aware, this matter was included in the speech from the throne. In addition, a resolution providing for an address to Her Majesty the Queen, related to an amendment to the British North America Act, has already been placed before this house. The proposed program will pose many complex problems and it will be particularly helpful to have this advisory council available while it is being established and brought into operation. The regulations and provisions under the family allowances and old age security programs will need to be reviewed from time to time with a view to relating them to changing needs and conditions.
The question of federal aid to encourage and assist in the development of homes for the aged and other types of domiciliary care has been raised in this house and elsewhere more and more as the years go by. It is a matter that deserves further consideration and is one on which the views of the national council of welfare will be sought.
As hon. members will note, the composition of the council is somewhat similar to that which has been provided for its counterpart in the health field. For example, the deputy ministers of the federal and provincial governments are to be members of the council and will bring to its meetings many years of experience in technical problems relating to the administration of social welfare measures in Canada. In addition, provision is made for ten representatives from outside of government. This will provide an opportunity to bring to the council the experience of many persons who have made a substantial contribution in the voluntary welfare field and to provide for citizen participation as well as geographic representation.

Health and Welfare Act
Mr. Speaker, I have put before you my hopes and expectations concerning an important undertaking that we feel confident will contribute in a significant way to social welfare progress in Canada. I am sure that it will enjoy the full support of all those interested in promoting the well-being of Canadians.
I should like to refer again to the other amendment to the Department of National Health and Welfare Act which as I mentioned earlier is of routine character. Specifically, it provides for the repeal of paragraph (g) section 5. As it now stands, this paragraph lists a number of statutes which at the time of the introduction of this act were within the duties, powers and functions of the minister. With the passage of time, this list has become out of date and must either be changed to reflect the current situation or deleted altogether. We have decided on the latter course since such a list does not affect the general authority of the minister and department and since, if it were retained, this would necessitate opening up the act for amendment whenever changes occurred in our programs.
The repeal of paragraph (g) section 5, therefore, is merely a step toward tightening up the existing legislation and will, I trust, be understood as such by the house.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to express my support for this bill I should like to say that, generally speaking, I think the statement the minister has made is one that will commend itself to the house. He has said that the bill seeks to do two things. First of all, it seeks to provide an amendment to delete a provision listing certain acts under the administration of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Second, it seeks to set up a national council on welfare. With regard to the first proposed amendment, I should like to say this. When the act was set up by the first minister of national health and welfare, , the late Hon. Brooke Claxton, there was a good reason for including various acts under the authority of the minister in the section of the act in which the enumerated powers and the enumerated legislative enactments were included.
At this time I should like to say that the Department of National Health and Welfare Act administered by the first minister of national health and welfare represented the humanitarian instincts of that hon. gentleman and his great administrative skills. At the time when the act was introduced it received wide acclaim from one end of the country to the other as well as in this House of Commons. It represented a new concept involving a new attitude on the part of the federal

government with regard to social welfare matters. In supporting this modification now being made I would not wish it in any way to be understood, nor would the minister nor would any other hon. member, that we were criticizing the original concept which the late Hon. Brooke Claxton had in mind. As his successor in that department, I think I can attest to his great qualities as an administrator and to the vision he had in establishing a department which increasingly is playing an extremely important role in the welfare of our country.
With regard to the second purpose of the amendment, namely the establishment of a national council on welfare may I say this. This is not an idea that is altogether new. It was made part of the declaration of social security for Canada by the Canadian welfare council itself on June 2, 1958. That declaration contains some 22 recommendations made *by the Canadian welfare council to the government of Canada and to the people of Canada generally, setting out various objectives in the social welfare field. Among them was recommendation 20 which reads as follows:
Machinery should be devised to ensure regular communication among provinces, and between provinces and the dominion government, on all welfare matters of common interest.
Recommendation 21 reads as follows:
The dominion government should establish a broadly representative body of competent persons, the purpose of which would be to keep under constant review all aspects of Canada's social security program and to advise on changes and improvements that may from time to time be desirable.
The council adds this commentary:
Because of the wide range and diversity of interests and programs in social security, it is essential that the dominion government should have ready access to the advice and counsel of persons, both in and out of government service, who are technically competent and experienced in matters relating to this field.
I join the minister in expressing the view that the dominion council of health which is intended to serve as a model for the new council, has indeed been a very successful body. As a matter of fact, I suppose the dominion council of health is the oldest body that serves to provide for continuous collaboration between the two senior levels of government in our country. Biannually the representatives of all of the provincial governments through their deputy ministers meet with the Minister of National Health and Welfare and his deputy minister, for the purpose of collaborating on matters of mutual concern and jurisdiction. As a former minister of national health and welfare, I can attest to the usefulness of the dominion council of health. I note that the minister

intends that the new national council on welfare shall, in addition to the provincial representatives and those representing the federal government be made up of not more than 10 additional persons. I presume the reason for the larger unofficial representation is that the minister wishes to take into account bodies which otherwise would not be represented, as well as to take into account geographical considerations. My recollection is that on the dominion council of health there were three persons representing bodies other than the provincial and federal government.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to clarify the powers of the trustee board of the Presbyterian Church in Canada. The legislation dealing with this trustee board is out of date. For example, it gives powers of investment to that board by reference to the type of securities in which a life insurance company, carrying on business in Canada, may invest its funds. In practice such a loose definition is not effective and it is proposed to clarify the legislation to make it clear that the power to lend its funds must be the same power as that given under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act, with this change, that there is no limit on the amount of funds that may be invested in common stocks.

Then there is a power asked for to retain investments. In the case of gifts to the church it is now a fact, as the law exists, that these securities would have to be sold if they did not meet the requirements for the investment of funds. The bill before the house asks permission to retain such investments, even though they are not in the form required by the investment provisions of the legislation.
Then there is the clarification of the powers of the board to deal with the provisions for pensions for ministers. As the legislation now stands, the trustee board must invest the funds used for this purpose for handling the pensions themselves. It is thought desirable that they also have power to make a contract with the annuities branch of the government of Canada, or an insurance company, or a trust company for the management of their pensions, in other words to purchase a pension contract and transfer its pension funds to the company providing the pensions.
Then there is another incidental change in the last provision of the bill dealing with clarification of the terminology used in the legislation.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Arnold Peters (Timiskaming) for Mr. Howard, moved the second reading of Bill No. C-18 to amend the House of Commons Act (internal economy autonomy).
He said: In moving this bill I should first explain that its purpose is to bring up to date a practice that has developed over a period of many years in the operation of the House of Commons. The original method of selection of the internal economy committee 27507-3-100i
House of Commons Act was formulated many years ago in Great Britain, and Canada, for no apparent good reason, has followed a similar method.
The Speaker of the house, of course, is in charge of the operations of the house, and by order of the Governor General, as found on page 15 of Votes and Proceedings for Thursday, September 27 there appears the following:
The Governor General transmits to the House of Commons a certified copy of an order in council appointing the Honourable Leon Balcer, Minister of Transport, the Honourable Gordon Churchill, Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Honourable George Clyde Nowlan, Minister of Finance, and the Honourable Ellen Louks Fairclough, Postmaster General, to act with the Speaker of the House of Commons as commissioners for the purposes and under the provisions of the one hundred and forty third chapter of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, intituled: An Act respecting the House of Commons.
We have no objection to the method used in the past. It has worked very well but we do feel it needs to be reviewed, as it has been reviewed in the United Kingdom, and that consideration should be given to the changing times and the changing necessities of the House of Commons as it affects members of parliament and others connected with it. We feel that Your Honour would be much better served if representation for the internal economy commission came from sources other than those now selected.
While it is generally agreed that all expenditures of money must be proposed by members of the government we believe that with respect to the operations of the House of Commons the guidance and advice of persons other than those appointed from the treasury benches should be sought. Some discussion has taken place on this matter outside the house and I refer to an article which appeared in The Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science, headed "The financial administration of the House of Commons," by J. R. Mallory of McGill University.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INTERNAL ECONOMY AUTONOMY
speechtext: What is the date of that?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INTERNAL ECONOMY AUTONOMY
speechtext:
February, 1957, I believe. On page 109 it states:
The present statutory basis for the internal economy commission is section 16 and 17 of the House of Commons Act which enjoin the governor general in council to nominate, at the beginning of each session of parliament, four privy councillors who are members of the House of Commons to act with Mr. Speaker for the purpose of financial administration of the House of Commons. The privy councillors so appointed are invariably ministers of the crown.
It goes on to say how this has been established in England and points out the similarity in methods applied in Canada over the years. It is interesting to note that going

House of Commons Act back in the history very little is really available to ascertain how these arrangements were made. I quote from the same document, on page 111:
The two volumes in the Macdonald papers in the public archives entitled "Committee of internal economy" are equally unhelpful, for they deal chiefly with the patronage to the various appointments in the House of Commons, decision on which seems always to have been referred to the prime minister. One can do no more than echo the considered conclusion of Professor Ward, that "Whatever the statute was intended to do (and its purpose is certainly not clear from the text), in practice the internal affairs of the House of Commons, in so far as such matters as personnel, size of establishment, and rates of pay were concerned, were in the sole control of the executive branch of the government". In terms of practical Canadian politics of the period they were indeed, but it is perhaps not unimportant that the arrangement paid lip service to a different concept. That the domestic arrangements of the house fell so completely under the shadow of the executive was due, as the surviving correspondence shows, not so much to the administrative structure as to the fact that successive speakers referred even the most trivial questions to the prime minister. Considering the position of the speakership in Canadian politics, this practice was perhaps inevitable.
Mr. Speaker, the report of 1954 of the select committee on house of commons accommodation in England made a number of recommendations which I think are worthy of consideration at this time. The recommendations were these:
1.	"... the time has now come when the duties of the commissioners should be entrusted to a more representative body of members with less onerous responsibilities outside the house than those borne by the commissioners, who with the exception of Mr. Speaker are all ministers .. . the commissioners should be replaced by a body of experienced members drawn from the house who would undertake not only the present functions of the commissioners with regard to staff, but also wider duties in relation to the accommodation and management of the house".
2.	The commission should consist of the speaker as chairman, and the leader of the opposition (or his deputy), the chancellor of the exchequer (or other treasury minister), the minister of works (or his parliamentary secretary), and "a suitable number" of other members, not less than nine in number, one of whom should be selected to be vice chairman by the speaker. The commission should be set up at the beginning of each parliament for the duration of that parliament.
3.	In addition to the present duty of the commissioners with regard to the salaries of officials of the house, the commission should advise the speaker on the estimates of the house, the allocation of accommodation, the library, facilities and services to "enable members to discharge their duties", and should control the arrangements for the kitchen and refreshment rooms.
4.	Items relating to expenditure in that part of the Palace of Westminster now borne on the votes of the ministry of works and other ministries should in future be borne on the vote of the house of commons.
5.	The commission should report annually to the house, and should in future be consulted in the appointment of the clerk of the house and the sergeant-at-arms (which are, as in Canada, crown appointments).

Mr. Speaker, some of these recommendations of course do not apply to the House of Commons of Canada. We, of course, do not have the same problem in the jurisdiction of the facilities as they have in the mother parliament, where the crown has ownership of some of these facilities and where the minister of public works is asked to make decisions on their behalf. But we do in Canada have many problems that are causing us difficulty. I suggest, respectfully, that we now have these difficulties because of the fact that all the advisers to Your Honour are members of the treasury benches. I suggest it may be a little bit like the housekeeping expenses of the normal family; if they find there is not enough money to go around, this may be a very good place to introduce methods of economy. We may, because of this, be under certain handicaps.
It has been suggested by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) that the members should be Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition or his appointee, the leaders of the other political parties in the house, a member representing the Minister of Finance and other members who would be appointed because of their long experience in the House of Commons and their familiarity with the particular problems. I believe that all hon. members will agree that the duties of cabinet ministers in our government have become increasingly demanding, and therefore it may be possible that they find this added responsibility something of a burden.
However, it seems to me that if we had a more representative body advising Your Honour, some of the things that would be included in the agenda for discussion and for some solution would be the problems that affect the press accommodation in this building, some of the problems that arise from day to day in connection with the facilities of the library and the fact that there could be additions made to the library which would be of great assistance to the members and which are not now provided. Certainly some arrangement would be made to assist members of parliament in the matter of research. It seems to me that facilities similar to those provided at the United Nations could well be installed in the House of Commons to allow for the establishment of studios for radio and television broadcasting from the house, thereby making it much easier for the news media to come to members of parliament and for the members to go to the news media.
Other matters could be presented and discussed on their merits in a much more satisfactory manner than is now adopted. It seems to me that many of the problems of staff could be better handled if there were

a more representative body advising the internal economy committee. I think this should include a more reasonable method of handling the staffs than the one we now have. Arrangements could be made on a more formal basis for employment on a year round basis of staffs that are now considered temporary, whether they were put into other employment in the periods when parliament was not in session or some other method were adopted. Our staffs have to work long hours and overtime, and this should be paid for as it is in other occupations and other fields. Holidays would either be given as they are in other fields, or if the committee and the house decided that the staffs should work on those days which would normally be holidays, they should be paid double time for that work. They should not be asked to take this time off on Saturdays, as happens at the end of a session. As hon. members probably know, the staffs are asked to take this form of compensation rather than the normal one.
In addition, I think that advice coming from a more representative body would lead to the protective staff of the house being given the security which police normally have. For example, they would be able to make arrests with the full authority of police officers. I believe there would be more favourable parking space allocated to those who work in the House of Commons and that the accommodation generally would be based not only on what it was considered we could afford but on recommendations made on the basis of what facilities were likely to produce the most effective operation of the House of Commons.
I wish to make it clear that I am not suggesting that in the past the commissioners or the internal economy committee have been negligent. However, I do believe that because of their other responsibilities it has been difficult for them to consider many of the problems which should be considered by such a committee. For this reason I hope the house will give consideration to the changes I have suggested in this bill and that, in consequence, representation on this committee will be on a much wider basis, reflecting all parties and all sections of the house. As I say, I hope some members will be chosen to serve on the committee simply because of their long connection with parliament and its operation. I hope the bill will be given a speedy passage in order that the satisfactory results which, I am convinced, will follow, may be self-evident to all hon. members as soon as possible.

House of Commons Act members of the privy council to be appointed as commissioners. Now he says that the cabinet should appoint the commissioners by order in council. I think this represents a conflict with the basic principle which the hon. member has in mind, if I gather the effect of the bill correctly, which is to take the appointments away from government and place them instead in the hands of the house. However, we realize that when he made his remarks he was acting on behalf of his associate, the hon. member for Skeena, who is not with us today, and perhaps, on reflection, he might think he had not come up with the correct alternative remedy after all.
It seems to me that in the presentation of this bill and in the arguments supporting it we have witnessed a vast piling up of a mountain of straw which has brought into being the appearance of a problem that does not really exist at all. It does not seem to me that any case has been made out for a change in the present system of the appointment of commissioners of internal economy of the House of Commons.
My experience in this field is as limited as that of the sponsor of the bill, or of his friend the hon. member for Timiskaming. I have witnessed the rare occasions upon which Mr. Speaker descends from his chair, sits among us in committee and answers questions on the estimates. I cannot recall in those debates that any serious criticism ever came forward suggesting that the affairs of the House of Commons were not being managed properly by His Honour and those commissioners appointed to advise him. I may be wrong, but my mind goes back over five or six years and I do not recall an instance where it could be said that the advice you were getting from your commissioners, Mr. Speaker, had led you or your predecessor astray. I realize the delicacy of your position, sir, inasmuch as you have to listen to us and hear us out when, no doubt, many things are on your mind which might be useful in this debate. Until the time comes when you take your place on the front bench later on, when your estimates are under consideration, perhaps you are at a disadvantage.
However, as I say, looking back over those years I cannot recall one instance which would buttress the case put forward by the hon. member for Timiskaming. Indeed, as the leader of the house so ably pointed out in the debate on March 6 of this year, the system has functioned very well over the years. It was not until the hon. member for Skeena came to this parliament that there was the suggestion that this system should be changed.

As I understand it, there had originally been a committee, I believe called the committee of contingencies, which concerned itself with the operations of the House of Commons. Then in 1878 the House of Commons by unanimous action set up the present system, and since 1878 nobody, perhaps with the exception of a high-flying intellectual has really questioned the effective operations of the commissioners of internal economy of the House of Commons. Furthermore, if I may so respectfully suggest, should there be any of what hon. members may feel are derelictions or "soft spots" in the administration of the House of Commons, it is incumbent upon them to come knocking at Your Honour's door and ask to be heard, whether they are asking you, Mr. Speaker, to see that there are more parking places allotted to members of parliament, or that there should be more protective staff, or more cleaning staff, or more waste paper baskets, or an extra telephone, or any of the other amenities the absence of which bother a member of parliament from time to time.
Mr. Speaker, I say that we have this remedy now. The commissioners, too, are all affable people, ready to hear the complaints and suggestions of those who work in the House of Commons. So it seems to me that the bill of the hon. member fails on two grounds. First, it does not remedy anything of an abusive nature; and second, there are other steps to be taken to enable members of parliament to make particular points. I do not think anyone can say that he has been given a rough hearing by Your Honour, by the Clerk of the house, by the Sergeant-at-Arms, or by any of the other officials who cater to our needs.
Since this is a somewhat esoteric subject, perhaps it would be interesting, Mr. Speaker, to note Beauchesne's reference to the work of the commissioners of internal economy in collaboration with yourself. This quotation is to be found at page 314 of Beauchesne's fourth edition:
The Speaker and four members of the privy council, who are also members of the house, are, by the governor in council, appointed commissioners of internal economy of the House of Commons. Their names must be communicated by a message from the governor to the house in the first week of each session of parliament. The powers of the Speaker for the purposes of this act are extended to last until the election of his successor by the next parliament. In the event of the death, disability or absence from Canada of the Speaker, during any dissolution or propagation of parliament,-
Mr. Speaker, I believe that word should be "prorogation", but "propagation" is Beauchesne's word. For those interested in the spelling, or possibly my mispronunciation, I am referring to page 314

-any three of the commissioners may carry the provisions of the act. The Clerk and Sergeant-at-Arms shall make estimates of the sums required for the service of the house and shall submit the same to the Speaker who may approve or alter them and who shall transmit them to the Minister of Finance for submission to council. They shall subsequently be laid before the house with the other estimates for the year. All sums of money voted by parliament shall be subject to the order of the commissioners or any three of them, of whom the Speaker shall be one.
This is a further interesting point.
Questions dealing with salaries paid the staff or with details about the management of the house's affairs should not be addressed to the Speaker from the floor of the house when he is in the chair.
I must say that that is a helpful point, and I am sure the house will not mind my belabouring it for a moment, because we often wonder where these rules and procedures come from, and we find them set forth succinctly in Dr. Beauchesne's work. The quotation continues:
He is bound-
That is, the Speaker is bound.
-to give any information sought by members when the legislation estimates are under consideration in committee of supply.
That was exactly the point I made earlier, that should a member want, for example, an extra parking space, another waste paper basket, or a telephone, and he feels that he has a legitimate gripe, he can ask Your Honour about it when you appear before us with your estimates in committee of supply.
Members who wish to be informed about the expenditures under the control of the house may either write to the Speaker or place on the order paper questions addressed to the commission of internal economy.
I might do that myself and ask why this particular page of Dr. Beauchesne seems to have several printing errors on it.
The answers will be prepared and tabled by the Clerk of the House who is the official secretary of the commission of internal economy.
So I suggest to the hon. member for Skeena that there are all sorts of obvious ways to meet his complaint. The practical step is simply to consult with the commissioners of internal economy or with yourself, Mr. Speaker, in order to solve any problem which any hon. member may have.
In a speech which should be commended to any student of this subject, the house leader on March 6 of this year, as reported on pages 1539 and 1540 of Hansard, set forth some of the work of this committee of 1867 and 1868, called, I think, the committee of contingencies. I should like to quote briefly from the house leader's speech as reported on page 1539:
The House of Commons dealt with 17 resolutions which were put forward in the third report of the committee of contingencies. It is interesting to note that they were concerned with matters of
House of Commons Act financial economy to be observed in the House of Commons. They dealt with the number of translators and the number of extra clerks that should be employed. They considered such things as the reception and distribution of the printed bills and other documents. They dealt with the subject of the post office and its management. They suggested that no clerk be stationed in the reading room, that there should be but two messengers and one labourer in the joint department on routine and printing, that there be but one messenger in the library and that no messenger be attached to the office of the Speaker's secretary or to that of the assistant clerk of the house.
I believe, sir, that possibly times have changed in that regard.
They set the salaries of various people employed by the House of Commons. They suggested that the nine pages, which was the number they had working in those days

Here I interject that the pages must have been run off their feet, because I believe we have a larger number now and they always seem to be scurrying about in this chamber.
-should receive $1.50 per day during the session. They suggested that the salaries of the two night watchmen should be fixed at $400 per annum, that the stationery supplied to each member of the house should not exceed in cost the sum of $15 for each session-
Mr. Speaker, let me just stop and conjure up in the imagination of the house the unhappy prospect of what would happen to the various propaganda mills which have been established should that limit of $15 be placed again on stationery.
-and should be delivered in a box on the first day of each session, and that no more be issued.
I imagine that one of the first things the commissioners of internal economy of those far away days heard about was the suggestion that hon. members be given more stationery.
