speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while this debate is undoubtedly not an urgent one, it is most interesting. I And the ideas put forward by the hon. member for Timiskaming on this subject quite helpful, interesting and positive in their approach. In debating a bill like this one, to discern what is the principle of the bill really presents a problem as the bill simply contains two clauses, namely clause 1 repealing section 16 of the House of Commons Act and clause 2 repealing section 18 of the House of Commons Act. There is no more in the bill. Hence to find the principle in order to debate it, I suppose we can only look at sections 16 and 18 of the House of Commons Act, interpret them and thereby develop the principle of the bill now before us.
Any measure which seeks to guarantee the independence of the House of Commons in its deliberations and in its work against the control of the government is a proper measure, and one which in my view deserves consideration and support. From the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming in his speech on this bill I take it that is what he was seeking to do. However, I am troubled about the bill itself in that it may not do what he put forward, I thought rather well, in his exposition of it. That is why I asked him the questions at the conclusion of his remarks.
Looking at the sections of the House of Commons Act to which I have referred, one observes that section 16 is the authority of the governor in council for appointing the internal economy commission of the House of Commons and it provides that the four privy councillors so named shall be commissioners for the purposes of this section, namely section 16, and sections 17 and 18. It is therefore well that we look at those sections. The balance of section 16 merely provides for the communication of the names and offices

of the commissioners by message from the governor in council to the House of Commons in the first week of each session. Then it provides that three shall be a quorum. Then it makes provision for what is to be done in the case of the death or absence of the Speaker.
Section 18, the other section being repealed -and I think this is the key of the whole provision-provides as follows:
All sums ot money voted by parliament upon such estimates or payable to members of the House of Commons under the Senate and House of Commons Act, are subject to the order of the commissioners, or any three of them, of whom the Speaker shall be one.
By that it will be seen that the control of parliament over the voting of money is clearly preserved in the existing act. However, what is of concern is that the expending of this money is subject to the order of the commissioners, all of whom must be members of the House of Commons and members of the privy council. Hence we have in fact control by the government of the actual expenditure of the money after it is voted by parliament. That parliament should have control over the voting of money is, of course, clear. It may not be questioned anywhere. But the narrow point at issue is whether, after that money has been voted by parliament, the control over its expenditure or the detail of its expenditure, parliament having passed on it, is left to the advice of the cabinet or comes, if the remarks of the hon. member sponsoring this bill were carried out, from a board or committee of the House of Commons representing all parts of the House of Commons as opposed to the government only. It seems to me that is the essence of the proposal and the question that would have to be considered.
If the change being asked for by the sponsor were to be brought about I should think that new provisions in substitution for sections 16 and 18 of the act would be required, as it is quite clear that the government appoints these four commissioners now under the authority of section 16 of the act. If that section is being repealed and if persons are to be appointed representing all parties, then the authority for that step should be provided. I should think that authority would best be provided by a method of appointing by resolution of the house. However, the method is open to discussion since the bill does not provide for any method. In other words, there is that defect in the bill, namely that it takes away the commission of internal economy and does not make possible the provision of a substitute body.
Section 16 of the act, by reference, incorporates section 17. Section 17 contains five subsections, which in essence, provide for the preparation of estimates each year by the Clerk of the House of Commons for those

parts of the staff whose duties come under his jurisdiction and similarly for the Sergeant-at-Arms. Then it is required that the estimates of the Clerk and of the Sergeant-at-Arms be submitted to Mr. Speaker for his approval and he has quite wide authority to approve and to make alterations. The actual section reads as follows:
(3) Such estimates shall be submitted to the Speaker for his approval, and are subject to such approval and to such alterations as the Speaker considers proper.
Then the section goes on to direct that the Speaker shall thereupon prepare an estimate of the sums requisite for the several purposes aforesaid, and shall sign the same, and that the estimates of the Clerk, Sergeant-at-Arms and the Speaker-the three sets of estimates- shall be transmitted by the Speaker to the Minister of Finance for his approval. Then it goes on to provide that they shall come before parliament in the ordinary way as part of the estimates.
It will therefore be seen that the function of this board of commissioners is advisory only to Mr. Speaker, or that the actual authority for the preparation of these estimates that come before parliament for parliament's approval resides in the Speaker. I would hope this is where it would always remain because parliament, as such, has control over these estimates and the voting of money.
Then, when we come to section 18 there is a point of real concern. It may well be that the advice, if I may use that term, given to the Speaker for the expenditure of the moneys voted by parliament could well come from such a committee as the sponsor proposes in so far as those things affecting the House of Commons are concerned, instead of the present commission which is really the government. It seems to me there is a real point there that should be considered. I must say that I do not regard the matter as of the utmost urgency because I have no special objection to the decisions of the commission on internal economy. However, I must say that while at times I have found some of these decisions rather distasteful I have no wish to make any point of that or to comment adversely on their decisions. Their decisions do not indicate a need for their replacement, so that there is no urgency for replacing them such as one might find in many other bills.
There is the point however that does affect the liberties or rights, if I may use that term, of the House of Commons, to have the management of its activities free from undue influence by the government. There is quite an argument to be made for that. I do not share the views of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), who seems to view the 27507-3-101
House of Commons Act matter as unimportant merely because it is academic-and I take it by "academic" he means not urgent at this time. I could not share his views about the perfection of the present system. I do not have his reluctance to make a change. For my part, I am quite prepared to accept a change if it can be brought forward in a form that will achieve some of the ideas expressed by the sponsor of the bill.
Unfortunately, the bill itself takes away what we have, as has been rightly said by the hon. member for Halifax, and does not put anything in its place; that is not my idea of the way to reform. My idea is that when you take away something that has been in use you should replace it with something that is better. The bill, unfortunately, omits the something which is better. I would hope that if the bill carries, something adequate by way of new provisions for appointment might be brought forward in the committee stage before real consideration would be given to the bill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL COUNCIL OF WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister does not propose any modification in the organization of his department through any amendment now being proposed in the bill before the house. The only proposed structural change has to do with the deletion of the provision which lists certain acts, some of which are not now in existence, which come under the function of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I assume that the government has given consideration to various suggestions which have been made by the Canadian welfare council, the congress of labour and other organizations in Canada as to the re-organization of the Department of National Health and Welfare, particularly in relation to the Department of Labour. The suggestion has been made that all welfare legislation of an insurance type, and other types, should come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He has not said anything about this. The suggestion has also been made that because of heavy unemployment the Department of Labour should be charged primarily with the responsibility of establishing a vigorous and dynamic employment service, and that the problems of insuring the unemployed should be allocated to the Department of National Health and Welfare. I take it that the minister, as spokesman for the government, does not share this view.
I am not now expressing my own preference. There are overlapping interests between the two departments. I merely mention this to show that the particular amendment offered does not go to the substance of the Department of National Health and Welfare Act.
The minister may have had an opportunity of perusing the statement made by Professor John S. Morgan on behalf of the Canadian welfare council, made some time in the month of April this year. In the opening part of that statement, Professor Morgan says:
The time has come to rethink and redesign our welfare services.
He points out that in industry, and to some extent in government, we have accepted the inevitable consequences of the industrial and technological revolution, but when the talk comes to welfare we still hear statements about public responsibility "that are so irrelevant to a wage-earning industrial society that they are as pathetic as they are dangerous." I think we will accept this statement about the responsibility of government in the modern industrial society to the problems of human welfare as being at the

base of the proposition for the proposed council. In this connection Professor Morgan points out:
I think we must recognize two important facts about welfare in a modern industrial society. The first is that all of us have needs that cannot be met without the collective resources of society as a whole and that any reasonable concept of welfare benefits includes all of us. The second is that government, representing the collective resources of the whole nation, is not merely a legitimate participant in the development of welfare services, but is the only effective instrument for the provision of preconditions of good welfare services and the larger part of those services.
Some may argue, and indeed I have seen the suggestion made in one of the more prominent daily newspapers, that the setting up of a council on welfare is a further unnecessary expansion of government activity and organization. I am not aware that the Glassco commission has said anything about this. In fact I am not aware that the Glassco commission has yet dealt with all of the services of the Department of National Health and Welfare. But lest there be anyone in this house inclined to think there is something in the suggestion that this is a further proposed organization that might well be dispensed with, we should remind ourselves of the pattern of the statutory welfare services in Canada on both federal and provincial account.
These services are provided by governments at all levels, and with specific welfare objectives. A great stride has been made in this area of activity in our country during the last 50 years. In 1913 the public expenditure on health welfare stood at $15 million, or about $2 per capita of the population. In 1959 and 1960 the corresponding figure was more than $3 billion, or about $166 per capita. Therefore public welfare services are now a major item of public service in Canada and if there is a justification, as I believe there is and was at the end of the second world war, for setting up an organization of the provincial governments and the federal government for the purposes of discussing common matters involving health there is a dollar justification for our interest in welfare expenditures. We must make sure that our plans are devised to meet the needs of the people, and that we take into account what the various governments at different levels are seeking to do.
I expect that the total welfare expenditures of $3 billion will more than compare with the total expenditures by governments in the field of health, apart altogether from proposed expenditures that would bring this total to a much higher figure, particularly if we adopt, as I hope we will adopt at the earliest possible moment, a provision for medical care insurance.

Mr. Speaker, may I briefly recapitulate. I think these amendments are desirable. We in the Liberal opposition will support them. We think they will strengthen the Department of National Health and Welfare Act. We believe that the suggestion which the government now makes first came from the Canadian welfare council. We think that a tribute should be paid to the work of this voluntary organization, not only for its general activities but for its specific recommendations about which I made some mention before adjournment.
While we approve the proposal of the minister, we are strongly of the view that it would be unfortunate if the minister were to use the device of the setting up of this council to postpone proposals now before parliament and which have been discussed generally in the country. It would be regrettable if, because this council was not going to be set up until next spring or late next winter, the excuse for no action was offered that nothing could be done until such time as the two senior levels of government could consider these proposals in the new council on welfare. Among these as I mentioned earlier, is the proposal for a contributory pension scheme based on the social security program of the United States. There is now on the order paper some indication of the government's present intention in this regard. There is standing in my own name a resolution urging this house to give consideration to the desirability of setting up a contributory pension plan based on the social security plan in the United States.
The government has before it all the information that it needs to set up such a plan. There is the monumental work in two volumes of Professor Clark which sets out the situation in a number of countries, particularly in the United States, with regard to contributory schemes providing for payments on a rising scale based on contributions made by the potential beneficiaries of the scheme. No delay need now take place in implementing, in the absence of a constitutional arrangement, some parts of this plan. This is particularly true in the case of the government because of its action in 1958, when before the elections of that year the Prime Minister announced the appointment of a royal commission under Professor ITewson to examine into the whole business of contributory pensions for Canada based on the social security model in the United States. We recall that Professor Hewson was unable to complete his assignment in the four-month period stipulated by

Health and Welfare Act the Prime Minister. Professor Clark, however, did make an exhaustive report. That report has been on the desk of the Minister of National Health and Welfare for over three and a half years now.

I am talking about the specific royal commission appointed by the Prime Minister about which nothing was done. I believe that if we really want to provide our people with a responsible system of old age security, one that will meet the economic needs of the moment, the way to do it is to recognize that we should adopt in Canada the principal features of a system that has now been in vogue in the United States for some time and which has been accepted by other countries since the introduction of this measure in the United States.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL COUNCIL OF WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indicated in the explanatory section of this bill, and it was also reiterated by the minister, that the main purpose of this measure is to establish a national council of welfare. I believe that the needs of the Canadian people in this particular field, and also an increasing social consciousness, demand that we use every legitimate means to the end that Canadians everywhere will be able to share in the accumulated wealth of this great nation of ours.
We also notice in the explanatory section that this measure does not propose to deal with the matter of health, because it is taken care of in another section of the act. Therefore it would indicate that we are going to
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).!

deal more specifically with the economic problem and the economic postion rather than with the health factor in our society. I am sure that, regardless of the name by which it is known, each political party represented in this house has as its main concern the welfare of the people of Canada. Our approach may be different and we may differ in the nature of the measures which we may feel are necessary in order to meet the need, but I trust that the sincerity of our motives, no matter where we may sit in the house, will not be open to question in this particular matter.
If this measure passes, Mr. Speaker, and the council is established, I believe we must guard against the possibility that the government may shrug its shoulders and more or less pass on to the council the responsibility that rightfully rests upon the government, for in the final analysis it is the government that is charged with the responsibility of promoting the welfare of all people within the bounds of Canada. It is not a matter of its assuming the position that in some way or other it must by handouts and various other means provide for all the needs of the people; but it must ensure that adequate provision is made and policies are promulgated that will make it possible for everyone to have their basic needs supplied.
I think that for too long we have been obsessed, possibly, with a philosophy of scarcity, while in reality we have moved forward into the area of production to the extent that we find it almost impossible to dispose of our goods. We have failed to develp an effective technique whereby the people across this great nation of ours would be able to provide for their own needs. Therefore, instead of sharing in the abundance that is ours in Canada, many of them are just getting by and many others are in the condition of poverty and absolute destitution. These conditions ought not to exist for anyone in Canada regardless of who he may be or wherever he may live. We believe that as the beneficiaries of the accumulated labour, skill and cultural progress of generations which are past, all have a claim on a share of the great inheritance that is ours.
There is one word of caution I should like to pass along this evening. Whatever the activities of this proposed council, the prerogatives of the provinces must be fully recognized. Once one step is taken in a field which is recognized as being primarily a provincial responsibility there is a tendency for another and yet another step to be taken. Thus we find that even if it is simply a matter of research and advice, the tendency will be to move further and further into provincial

jurisdiction. For this reason I suggest that the activities and operations of the proposed council should be taken while being fully conscious of this danger. I believe the statement made by the minister to the effect that the deputy ministers of the various provincial departments will be represented on this council is reassuring, because that will be a fairly adequate safeguard in this connection.
There are several basic principles which undergird the economic condition we would like to see in Canada. First, we believe it is the right of all free Canadians to participate in the collective benefits which have accrued to our society. Perhaps this has been forgotten; perhaps in the past we have not recognized it. But as we look back over the tremendous developments which have taken place through the years, when we think of the position we have reached today in the field of production and when we think of the advances in science and technology it is clear that we can enjoy the advantages which exist today because of the contribution which was made to the development of this great heritage by past generations. Therefore I think it is the right of every Canadian to be able to participate in the results of this development.
The second principle is this: there is a need for the development of an economic system which will make this participation possible. I am sure we all understand by this time that this particular group has been emphasizing this factor down through the years. As we consider the present situation-and I intend to summarize-we find we have no problem as far as the production of goods for our people is concerned; and as far as the market is concerned, the potential market is there. The difficulty is that instead of making progress in this field, as we have done in so many others, we have not as yet reached a satisfactory answer to the problem of distribution. Until we meet and solve that problem we shall be faced continually with problems of welfare and how people are going to keep alive in various circumstances and situations of life. This is one of the great reasons why we must give particular attention to the development of an adequate financial and economic system which will meet the needs of our people.

Health and Welfare Act
There is a third factor connected especially with the subject under discussion tonight, and it has to do with the provision of additional resources to meet the needs of those who find themselves in an especially difficult economic situation-those who in spite of all the labour and sacrifices entailed in the building of this nation have not been able to assure for themselves an adequate income in their declining years. We are indebted to the pioneers and builders of this nation; and these people, in turn, are looking to us in time of need.
We in this group maintain that assistance should be forthcoming not as charity or as a dole but as a right to the citizens of Canada regardless of who they are. I believe we can look to some of the provinces in western Canada to find an indication that on the provincial level there is a recognition of the responsibility that is ours toward the pioneers of this nation. Those provinces have made provision for payments additional or supplementary to those now received under old age security or other allowances. There was a reference made to this subject by the hon. member for Essex East. He said he hoped the national government would not take the setting up of this council as a means of bypassing its responsibility to fulfil promises which were made in the past election campaign. I should like to say this: I trust that when this matter comes to the attention of the government the provision made for those who are in need will be a little more generous and will be granted with a little more alacrity than that which was given by the Liberal government when it was in office, because that government did not indicate with any too clear a voice that it was willing to meet its obligations in this field.
Not only do we think of those in receipt of pensions of various kinds, but we think of those who are physically and mentally unable to provide for their own livelihood. Here again we believe society must accept its responsibility and make adequate provision for these people. Again, there are those who through no fault of their own find themselves unable to secure gainful occupation in our society. I mention some of these groups in order to indicate that there are certain categories of our citizens who require additional assistance in order to meet their economic needs. I have here a copy of the first report of the Christian doctrine of wealth committee of the congregational union of Scotland presented to the assembly at Dundee on May 10, 1962. One of the observations made in this report is as follows:
Whenever paid employment ceases to function adequately as a means of providing livelihood.

Health and Welfare Act
alternative means must be offered to prevent the suffering and human wastage that arise from poverty and want.
It seems to me that this underlines our responsibility in this particular field. I should like to give one more brief quotation from this same report. As one of the objects of a social economic system, this report suggests-
-the elimination of insecurity and fear and consequent selfish materialist values, so that the individual human being may be able to live with dignity and self respect.
We welcome this particular bill. We believe that it will be of real assistance to have a committee or a council such as this to study these various matters and to bring in recommendations. I believe it is true that we must have an integrated plan with respect to our responsibilities in these particular fields. As it is now, we have a great many of them which do not dovetail together too well, but which have been put forward to meet particular situations at various times. But I believe the time has come when an integrated plan must be provided whereby all of those in particular need may have their needs taken care of. I think a reappraisal of the principle of joint programs would be a good thing, for in this respect I think there is much to be desired. The minister indicated that homes for the aged would also come in this particular category. I suggest that all these problems require thorough consideration. We believe that the proposed council will be able to give them the study which they deserve, and give the assistance which the membership of that council would be well qualified to give. So, Mr. Speaker, as I have said, we welcome this particular measure and will give it our support.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL COUNCIL OF WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic party is pleased to give its support to this bill. Like others who have spoken, I would say there is other legislation in this field we should like to see introduced in this session of parliament, but that statement does not detract from our readiness to welcome what is proposed in the legislation now before the house. As the minister has pointed out, and as is clear from the bill, two proposals are made. The first is a routine one, which is really just a matter of tidying up one of the sections of the act; it calls for no further comment at this time. The other and more substantial proposal in the bill is, of course, that to set up a national council of welfare. As I have already indicated, we welcome this proposal wholeheartedly.
I should like to say at the outset that the proposal to set up a national council of welfare composed of civil servants and others working in the welfare field gives us the opportunity to pay tribute in this house to the tremendous service rendered to the cause of social welfare by people other than those of us who get elected to public bodies. All of us in this parliament know the part that members of parliament and members of legislatures play in this field. We sometimes have arguments as to which parties have played the greater part, but we can carry on that argument at some other time. Tonight I should like to pay tribute to the many devoted public servants in departments like the Department of National Health and Welfare here in Ottawa, and to their counterparts at the provincial level, as well as to those at the municipal level, who are working in this field. I would join with the minister, the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Fraser Valley in paying tribute to those in the voluntary agencies who have done a great deal to push forward the cause of social welfare. I think of those who work in our schools of social welfare. I think of the Canadian welfare council, to which reference has been made. I think of labour bodies, farm organizations, church organizations, and many groups of citizens who discuss social welfare matters, make proposals, and give support to the whole idea of advancing the cause of social welfare.
I am glad that even as we have a body of this kind in the field of health, we are now going to have a national council of welfare to study these matters, to do what it can to bring about co-ordination in this field, and to make recommendations as to further steps which might be taken. However, even though this measure is a good one and one we welcome, we too do not want it be an excuse for inaction on the part of the

government. But that is no reason why we should not give this measure our full support, for parliament is still here and as members of it we are still in the position to remind the government of its responsibility to bring in legislation in the social welfare field.
Another concern which has been expressed was that uttered a few moments ago by my hon. friend from Fraser Valley, namely that the responsibilities of the provinces in this field should not be overlooked. As I understand it, that is one of the reasons for appointing this national council of welfare and for putting on it representatives of the provinces as well as of the federal government. As I understand the measure, the idea is that there can be steady discussion among the various groups of social welfare programs so that the rights and the responsibilities of the various levels of government may be kept in view. In other words, Mr. Speaker, despite my sharing with the hon. members who have preceded me in the debate the views about this body not being an excuse for inaction on the part of the government, I see no reason why we should not welcome it wholeheartedly. I do so, and express on behalf of this party the hope that it will, as did the dominion council of health, do a good job in the welfare field.
Mr. Speaker, I have enjoyed listening to the speeches made thus far on second reading of this bill. I think this debate is a very effective antidote to some of the arguments which appear in editorials in some of our newspapers and other publications. It has become almost a popular indoor sport to say that we have carried this idea of the welfare state too far. I do not agree with that view, and I was glad to hear hon. members like the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Fraser Valley joining with the Minister of National Health and Welfare in asserting that there are new areas into which we can yet move; and that there are improvements of things that are already on the statute books for which we should work. Even if some people decry the welfare state, and even though there are further advances required in the organizing of society in the way that it ought to be, I suggest that one of the finest marks of our time is the extent to which we have moved toward the welfare state. It is one of the most human and most decent things we have done, our trying to find ways of distributing at least to some extent the wealth we produce so that there will be a minimum of want or suffering amongst our people. 1 repeat that in my view it is one of the finest marks of our society, that we have accepted the principle
Health and Welfare Act that older people should enjoy dignity in their declining years; that we have accepted the principle that there should be some equalization of the incomes of our people through programs such as family allowances, disabled persons allowances, unemployment insurance and unemployment assistance.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these things are not just palliatives. They are not just things which should have been brought into being because of necessity. These are things which mark us as human beings, as people who can be concerned about our fellow citizens. If we are to get credit for being a decent and human twentieth century society I suggest that we must extend the idea of seeing to it as a nation, as a society, that we use our wealth to raise the living standards of all our people.
If I may digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. I think we must not only accept the welfare state and extend its principle, but that the day will come when we shall be obliged to achieve a welfare world -or we shall have no world at all. In other words, just as I feel that it is our responsibility in Canada to see that our older people, our younger people and those in between who are unable to look after themselves get their rightful share of what we are able to produce, also I think the day will come when as a world we shall be obliged to organize our economies, our trading and our governing of ourselves around the world so that there will not be a situation in which two thirds of the world's people go to bed hungry every night. I suggest that the welfare state is not something that we should go back on; rather, it is something from which we should move forward to an even better era for our people and for mankind the world around.
I hope these editorial writers who think we have gone too far with the welfare state and who say so in our newspapers, magazines and other periodicals, will note the unanimity of the four parties in this house tonight as we have taken part in this debate welcoming the setting up of a national council of welfare and welcoming the idea of going forward in this field. Sometimes these people who write against the welfare state or the welfare programs we have, imply that by some strange method, because we are paying better old age pensions today than was the case 30 years ago and because we are paying benefits under certain other programs, somehow we are using up resources or running ourselves into debt or causing the exchange crisis or whatever other trouble we may have. I should just like to point out that our senior citizens are not getting food,

Health and Welfare Act clothing or shelter that does not exist. They are not getting something that is a charge on the future. They are simply getting a small share of the goods and services that are being produced right now. There are other things that happen in our society and in our economy which are a tax upon the future or which mortgage the future of our economy. However, welfare programs do not do that. Welfare programs merely result in the people who need a decent break now getting their share of the goods and services we are producing right now at this very time.
So, Mr. Speaker, I welcome not only the introduction of this measure and the idea that we are to have a national council of welfare, but I welcome most warmly the debate that has taken place thus far. I am not worried about the crossfire there may have been and the little bit of political partisanship that has been injected into the debate. There may be some more of it before it is over. However, the thing that is significant is that from all four parties in this house there has been support for the idea of moving still further in the field of welfare. This is good, and I hope the editorial writers of this country will take note.
It has been suggested that one of the purposes of this council will be to co-ordinate the activities in this field of the various jurisdictions in this country. That is good. It had been suggested that another of its functions will be to study the various programs we now have and to make recommendations as to improvements that might be made. That also is good. I think they all need to be improved. I agree with those who have asserted already that there should be no delay, whether or not there is an election coming, in a further increase in the amount paid under the Old Age Security Act.
In my view the fact that there is on the order paper a motion calling for an amendment to the British North America Act regarding contributory pensions should not be an excuse for nothing else being done in the field of old age pensions at this session. The resolution effecting an amendment to the British North America Act may just lie on the order paper for weeks or months to come, for all we know. However, the fact is that right now we could afford and should have an increase in the pension paid under the Old Age Security Act and under the Old Age Assistance Act to at least $75 a month. I hope this will be done. I hope there will be improvements in the other plans, in unemployment assistance, in family allowances, in the Blind Persons Act and in the Disabled Persons Act. As I say, I hope we can get action on these matters without being obliged to


wait for recommendations from the national council of welfare. However, I also hope that the fact that we set up this council will suggest that we recognize that there are still other areas into which we might move.
I think, for example, of housing for senior citizens, something that has been mentioned tonight. This is an area which we have just begun to scratch. I think also of the whole question of the changes that are taking place in our society as married women join the working force, as more mothers go out to work. I know the kind of problems these developments create. However, it seems to me that, instead of just deploring these changes that take place, as some people do, we should recognize the changing patterns of society and should try to find programs which will cope with these changes. We may be obliged to define programs that will provide for assistance for the care of children and for assistance to mothers who must go out to work, assistance to families needing help in times of illness. We may be obliged to find other kinds of programs to assist people in these new situations. I am glad we are to have this national council of welfare to look at some of these new areas.
I have had the real privilege of being in this place across a good many years and I can recall the attitude there was some years ago toward some of the programs that are now on the statute books. I can recall a number of them but I shall mention just one. My good friend the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) will corroborate my story if that should be necessary, and if it is incorrect I am sure that he will tell me so. I can remember when the campaign from the floor of parliament first began for some pension or other kind of assistance to disabled persons. This plea was made from a number of quarters in this house, mainly by individual members. For a long while there seemed to be resistance to the idea. Sympathy was expressed, but it was a new idea and those who were in charge in those days, while they expressed their sympathy, did not quite see how it could be done.
Then, on one occasion, one of those disabled persons happened to write a letter, a personal letter, to the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent. As I understand it, that personal letter just happened to touch the heart of Mr. St. Laurent. It made him feel that something should be done about this. As I understand it, from then on things began to move. The idea was looked at in the department, and by the cabinet, and in due course the campaign succeeded. We got a Disabled Persons Act. We are used to it now. It is difficult now to look back and realize that there ever were these

technical or procedural difficulties. It is difficult to realize now that at one time even the experts of the day could not quite see how it could be done. Mind you, there are some real improvements needed in the Disabled Persons Act. The way in which it is now worded, the way in which it is now administered, a person has to be almost unable to move or even to feed himself in order to qualify under it. However, at least it is there and can be improved.
The point I am making is that within the parliamentary life span of some of us who are in this House of Commons, we have seen new ideas catch on and be written into legislative form. I hope that in this field the national council of welfare will do some real work, some real study, some real research and will come up with suggestions as to ways and means in which we might extend our thinking on social welfare. Welfare, Mr. Speaker, is no longer just relief. Welfare is no longer just a way of keeping some unfortunate people alive. Welfare, the sharing of our production has become a way of life. Welfare has become the means whereby we use a portion of the wealth that we are able to produce to see to it that all our people have a decent standard of living.
One of the other areas in which I think we shall have to move is that of maintaining a minimum standard of income. I appreciated the reference made by the hon. member for Essex East to the statement on social security for Canada which was prepared by the Canadian welfare council in 1958. One of the suggestions in that document was that we should find ways and means of guaranteeing to our people a minimum standard of income.
So, Mr. Speaker, the job is not done because we have old age pensions. The job is not done because we have half a dozen welfare programs on the statute books of Canada or on the statute books of our provinces. We have just begun. We have the principle established that it is the responsibility of our society so to organize its economic activities that people can have a decent standard of living. It is our job to carry through, and this of course involves some real hard thought on the part of all of us as to how we are going to do it.
We in this party feel that it is going to require democratic social economic planning to raise our production to the highest possible level. I do not share the view of the hon. member for Fraser Valley when he says we have completely solved the problem of production. If we are going to provide enough goods and services for a good standard of living for our people, if we are going to provide enough goods and services to raise the living standards of mankind the world around,
Health and Welfare Act including the nearly two billion who are hungry tonight, we have to go a great deal farther in the matter of organizing our economy so that we produce sufficient goods and services to meet the challenge of our time. In addition to producing goods and services, we have to find ways and means of distributing them equitably with an eye, as I say, to a decent standard of living.
This debate does not solve all these problems. The setting up of this national council of welfare does not mean that the morning after it is established these problems will be solved. But I do say, Mr. Speaker, it is a good thing we are having the council. I think it can do a good job and it should have the support of all of us. I like the kind of people who are going to be on it, the experts in the field, devoted civil servants who have given their lives to the task. When we get into committee, I should like to find out who the ten non-governmental people are to be or from what areas they are to come. They will perhaps represent labour, agriculture, business and the Canadian welfare council. I like it if people of that sort are going to become members of this body. But most of all, I like the fact that this debate is an antidote to the talk there is in some newspapers about welfare. Despite the progress we have made, the time has come to take a step forward. That is why we support the proposal to set up the national council of welfare and move ahead in this important field.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL COUNCIL OF WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not believe I need to say, because it has been said from this side already, that we approve of the idea contained in this bill. Any disappointment I might voice would be in the direction of the lack of principles or guideposts indicated here. Perhaps it is understandable that they are not spelled out in the bill, but I am disappointed that the minister himself did not spell them out for us. This entire question of welfare is not one which ever remains static. It is in a state of continued evolution as our new society and economic progress continually change and evolve. The suggestion, therefore, that at any time anything of this kind can be completely solved or that we should perhaps reach fixed goals, as has been indicated by my hon. friend who comes from my own province, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, is completely misleading. To say that what was possible today should have been possible 50 or 100 years ago, is just not a true statement. These things change -abilities, knowledge, economic possibilities -as time goes by.

Health and Welfare Act
I do feel that the minister is to be complimented for introducing a bill of this kind at this time. In spite of that fact, however, I feel some guiding principles should have been laid down; there should have been some explanation given for the benefit of those people who will be administering this measure. The kind of thing I am suggesting here is perhaps the kind of thing for which we have been criticizing this government, the lack of ability to grasp the necessity for using a budget as an economic instrument. It is the kind of thing that guides and assists the economy, rather than the method of 100 years ago when the government just accumulated bills and expenditures and introduced a budget at the end of the year to rover them.
I believe our welfare responsibilities, our ability to assist in these areas, are limited to the extent that our economy can support them. This is two parts of one element. There is the idea that we must maintain a high level of welfare so that we can say none of the people in our society are living at such a low level that they drag the rest of us down. However, there is a limit to the ability to pay, and therefore our economic structure must be taken into consideration. I would have thought that economists in our age would think in terms of the ability of any economy in this modern age to syphon off a measure of wealth in order to make sure that the people at the lower level of income do not drag us down. These are things for economists to discuss and clarify and find out. They are things for experts to work with. If the minister would only think of these things he would be well advised to tell the people who form part of this committee that these are guideposts they must use in order to assess their ability, in terms of dollars, and in terms of the economy as a whole to support the measures they may recommend.
Just to illustrate what I called evolution a moment ago, I find this in "Le Conseil du Bien-etre en notre millieu"-and I may say I heartily endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he stated what I think should be repeated again and again, that we owe a great deal to those men and women who have participated not only in the national welfare council but in the provincial welfare councils:
(Translation):
May I quote from the pamphlet entitled "The Welfare Council and Our Environment".
Some 40 years ago there began in Canada, and particularly in the province of Quebec, a vast industrialization movement, the effects of which are still being felt today. Accompanied by a growing urbanization, they have brought about several new social problems, while destroying some of the


previous structures of mutual help and assistance and weakening the traditional parochial organization.
Save for the reference to the traditional parochial structures, the same principle applies to other areas of Canada as well.
The economic and social changes resulting from these two movements, industrialization and urbanization, are to be seen in, among other things, a decreasing number of families owning their own house, insecurity in employment, unemployment and an inadequate salary in relation to family responsibilities, the scattering about of families and outside work for women. The advent of a different way of life has also brought about new requirements such as a better education, the need for a technical training and the desire for a higher standard of living.
During the following years, as it became more and more necessary to get together, organizations were created with the purpose of working for the social welfare of the country.
The report entitled "The Financing of Welfare Councils", and dealing with social welfare of the province of Ontario, states the following:
This new role-*
The reference is to the groups, and to the financing of those groups.
That new role, designed to integrate planning in the field of health, welfare and leisure, has resulted in the expansion of the councils' program and in the creation of the present need for increased financial resources, as well as concern about the importance of sources of revenue which will be available in the future.
In the last few years, the public sector has taken on the responsibility of making available an increasing proportion of those funds.
(Text):
As a result of this evolution and the great work done by these voluntary organizations, I believe we are in a position today to make one of the greatest steps ever made in this field. I do not say, as do our friends on the far left, that this should have been done 50 years ago, nor do I say as do our friends on the extreme right, that this can only be done by private enterprise. These are all things which have been accepted in Canada as forming a basic principle in our society, as a principle in our economics and a principle in our system of government.
There is not a single government in this country, whether it be Conservative, Social Credit, or C.C.F. such as in Saskatchewan, which does not accept as a fundamental principle of its duty the idea that social welfare is a part of our everyday living. Every day the public authorities, because of the complex social system in which we live and the complex economic system in which we find ourselves, necessarily find themselves becoming more and more involved in matters of social welfare.

I think the minister could assist those people who will administer this act by laying down some of these principles and some of these ideas, and by suggesting necessary improvements requiring immediate attention.
The question of disability pensions has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Provisions regarding disability pensions have been on our statute books for some time now. Perhaps there might have been an excuse at the very outset for being a little tight in the interpretation of those provisions, but I believe the time has come when there should be a much broader interpretation of what we mean by disability pensions in order to assist those people who are really disabled even though they may be able, but only able, to walk about. The present interpretation is much too rigid, and perhaps I might do like the member for Winnipeg North Centre and quote myself.

speechtext:
I refer to a speech I made in the Manitoba legislature a few years ago when we complained bitterly about the interpretation and application of the provisions regarding disability pensions in terms of their rigidity.
The minister might also take into consideration the fact that during the last few years, and unfortunately it is a relatively few years, we have finally recognized the difficult position in which we have placed the original Canadians. I speak of the Indians and Metis, and not mainly of those who are on reservations but those who are on the fringes of the reserves and who suffer most because they cannot get government assistance. Their suffering is increased also because, let us face it, while we condemn people outside this country for racial discrimination, we are often as guilty as any outsider in that respect, and these people suffer on that account.
However, I do believe a great deal of work has been done in this regard by welfare councils throughout the country. There is a sincere attempt being made to do something constructive about the problem, and I would recommend to the minister that he induce the administrators in the Indian affairs branch to come up with suggestions that would assist our red brothers to emerge from the ghettos, or reserves as we call them, and take their rightful part in modern Canada.
There is another area in which the minister could be helpful, and it concerns new Canadians, those people who have arrived in this country from outside and who find useful occupations for themselves and start life afresh in Canada. Very often, through circumstances
Health and Welfare Act beyond their control, they find themselves without a job and with family difficulties. In most cases they discover that they must move to other areas or other spheres in order to attempt to start a new life once more. Many of those people are in difficulty at present and they are not receiving the kind of assistance they need. Even though financial help is quite often available to them that is not the kind of assistance they require. What they need is guidance and assistance in relocating themselves.
Another area in which the minister might do some useful work is the displacement of workers because of automation. This is a problem which has only begun to hit us in recent years and much human suffering results from it. This is a question which is a little wide of the bill, but perhaps the members of this council could find some means of making suggestions that would assist in this field. I myself would make one suggestion in that I think it is a matter for education and adjustment instead of welfare. But here again, during this difficult adjustment period even if we do give these people an opportunity to retrain while they can still carry on and provide a living for their families, there is still an area where a council of this kind can render very useful service

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to support this bill to set up a national council of welfare. I think this is a wonderful move. There is no denying the fact that for far too long welfare has been far too much dependant upon the political whims of the politicians who in the long run so often evaluate these matters by the number of votes that might be secured. No one denies the inequality and the great variations that exist in this area today. There are great variations in the old age pension. We all know of these. For instance, a couple may live in the country in a low cost area. They may have a few hens or a cow and get along very well on their allowance. But a couple living in the city may pay out in rent per month for a couple of rooms the total of the taxes paid in the whole year by those people living in the country. Often the people living in the city in the high cost areas find themselves in very serious circumstances.
Then, again, in my opinion the disability pension is far too severe in its application. People who are unable to work because of physical or mental disabilities, or who in other words are unemployable, should be eligible for this pension. There are variations here. For example, a man may lose his leg. If that man was engaged in earning his living at physical work, he would be severly handicapped. But the fellow who loses his leg and has been doing clerical or professional work may find his income cut very little. As I have said, a fellow with his leg off may suffer a total disability. Of course, funds could be

applied for the retraining of such a man and perhaps we could get him back to the position where he is self-sustaining. There are a number of problems connected with baby bonuses and mothers allowances. Again, there are high cost areas and low cost areas, and the earning power of the various mothers varies. The same consideration applies to pensions for the blind. There are very capable blind men who are able to earn more money than some of us who have our sight. These are all matters for consideration.
Then I should like to see a better deal for our older people. I should like to see them left in their homes as long as possible. Many of them, as they get more feeble, are unable to look after their homes as they should. They are unable to provide the hot meals which are so necessary. I would suggest that the board give careful consideration to providing social aid workers to go into these homes, tidy them up, do the things that the older people find themselves unable to do and, when necessary, provide and cook a hot meal a day. I am sure that if we look into the financial side of all this it would represent a saving to us. Not only that, but it would allow these people to retain their selfrespect and a stable emotional outlook in the declining years of their lives. Many of these people deteriorate mentally at a more rapid rate when they are transferred to old people's homes than they would if they had been left in familiar surroundings. They become problems. From the humanitarian standpoint, I suggest that this point be given careful consideration.
I should also like to deal very briefly with families which have been living on welfare from one generation to another. I think there was a survey made in the city of Winnipeg which showed there were families who for five generations had been living on welfare payments. I want to say that it is a blot on our civilization and on our Christianity that we should permit young people to grow up in this country doomed to live on welfare payments for the rest of their lives. These young people must be salvaged from those homes and trained to become useful citizens. As I say, there are many serious questions awaiting the attention of this board. I congratulate the government for bringing this matter to the attention of the house because I feel that these inequalities in the interest of humanitarianism must be resolved.

Health and Welfare Act through the establishment of the national council of welfare. When we learn that on the federal, provincial and municipal levels in 1960 the sum of $3 billion was expended on social welfare services, amounting to $166 per capita, it is evident that social welfare is a very important question in this country.
I think the establishment of a national welfare council as proposed in Bill C-4 is a necessary step today because the present government has no national welfare policy that we can see. The Liberal attitude to social security has always been clear, and the record of the Liberal party in the field of social welfare is a most enviable one. As the former minister of national health and welfare stated this afternoon, every piece of social legislation on the statute books of Canada has been enacted by a Liberal government.
The time has come to reconstruct our welfare services. In the fields of industry and education, revolutionary measures have already been adopted to bring our practices up to date but when discussions are held in the realm of welfare we still hear statements about public and government responsibilities which are out of date in the wage-earning society we have in Canada in the present day. We must realize that all of us have needs which cannot be met except by the collective resources of society and that government is not merely a participant in the development of welfare services but also an effective instrument for the provision of certain necessary preconditions for adequate welfare legislation. Most important, I think this government must realize that the essential condition of welfare is a healthy economy. A government which allows itself to ignore the alarming unemployment situation which has existed in this country for the past five years is only aggravating the social welfare needs of the people. Welfare services alone cannot cure the cancer of a defective economic and social policy of the present administration.
In spite of the government's pleasant reassurances that Canadians never had it so good, I meet in my daily medical practice in the richest city of the richest province of Canada numerous sad examples of poverty. In our society today we witness the need of private and individual intervention in the welfare field. Individual citizens are called upon, unfairly, I think, to carry the burden of preventable illness, untreated sickness, unrehabilitated mental disability.
All of us in this house should be concerned with the nation's well-being. In this age welfare services should be related to the national level of economic prosperity and to a decent standard of living. In Canada, our minimum wage laws are inadequate and a

Health and Welfare Act large section of the working community is existing on a substandard wage. In my constituency of Parkdale I know women who are paid the scandalous sum of 85 cents an hour. We must have in this country adequate minimum wage laws and be able to enforce them. Then we shall be able to figure out welfare benefit levels on a proper basis. Frequently we see married women forced to go out to work in order to keep up a decent standard of living for their families. There is another great need in the field of social welfare and it has to do with the government's responsibility to rehabilitate those who are disabled. But social service programs should eventually be designed to prevent or even to anticipate social problems. It is in this field that welfare education is so necessary.
Here let me mention the need for family education, which should include preparation for marriage, family formation, home nursing services, recreational activities, and the care of elderly members of the family. We in this house must also deal effectively with the justifiable complaints about the present inadequate old age pensions and disability pensions. The cost of living index has risen every year since 1957, and last month reached a record high. We must admit that it is unfair to force our senior citizens without income and substantial savings to subsist on a mere $65 a month pension which starts at the age of 70. Moreover, there are many widows and unmarried women who have written or telephoned me to say they have a very hard time to eke out a living on $65 a month at the age of 70. They all stress the fact that from the age of 60 they already feel a financial burden. There is also a great need for income protection insurance during illness and for portable contributory pensions, and in my humble opinion we will have to reorganize our entire welfare services in the federal field. We need leadership from the federal government. We need a national welfare program, and I think it is high time that Canadians got leadership in this important field.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I will give the business for tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, and we will see what progress we make. We shall take third reading of Bill No. C-3, and then we will move into supply to consider the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

I wonder if the minister is aware of the fact that, of course, third reading of the bill is debatable. An unconditional undertaking was given by the Prime Minister that the agriculture estimates would be available tomorrow, so I wonder if the minister would not consider holding up the third reading of Bill No. C-3?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Third readings go through, 90 out of 100 times, in a matter of seconds.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
This is the one hundredth
time.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In other words, you want to debate third reading tomorrow?

I do not believe there is any need to consider what anyone wishes to do. There is a right to debate third reading. After giving an unconditional undertaking to bring the estimates forward, the government should not seek to impose any kind of closure on that unconditional undertaking in a manner in which I am sure the minister did not intend, but would have the effect of denying the opportunity to take advantage of the undertaking.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman talk about closure in this instance? It is just normal practice, having third reading. Who is suggesting closure in this instance?
I am, Mr. Speaker.

I would submit to the minister leading the house that the Prime Minister gave an undertaking the other day, when we wanted to discuss this matter of certain proposals regarding the Canadian wheat board, that an opportunity would be given on Wednesday. I would point out to the minister that Wednesday is only a half day and that the usual routine proceedings on orders of the day will take part of the afternoon. If, in addition, we have third reading of Bill No. C-3, which I think is likely to be debated, then this means there will be virtually no time to carry out the undertaking which the Prime Minister gave. I would urge the minister to reconsider this matter of introducing third reading of Bill No. C-3 tomorrow afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I must point out, Mr. Speaker, that this is not changing in any shape or form any decision or agreement made by the Prime Minister. There will be plenty of opportunity-at least I thought so- to have the third reading and then go on with the estimates, but if there is a desire on the part of hon. members, as has now been expressed, to have a lengthy debate on third reading of the bill, then I presume we can make other arrangements.
It being four minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, November 14, 1962
